mainEntity.name: How long does kratom withdrawal last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most physical symptoms begin 12 to 24 hours after the last dose, peak around days two to four, and ease within 7 to 10 days. Low mood and cravings can linger for weeks to months during post-acute withdrawal.

On its own it is rarely life-threatening, but it can involve high blood pressure, a racing heart, dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea, and severe low mood. Medical supervision makes it safer, especially when other substances are involved.

Kratom is not a controlled substance in Canada, so possession is not illegal. However, Health Canada has not authorized it for human consumption, so selling it as an ingestible product or making health claims is against the rules, and the market is unregulated.

mainEntity.name: Does Suboxone help with kratom withdrawal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, yes. Buprenorphine-naloxone works on the same opioid receptors kratom targets, so it can ease withdrawal and cravings. Many clinicians use it to help people stop kratom, especially when dependence is significant.

mainEntity.name: Can I quit kratom cold turkey at home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some people with mild use manage it, but cold turkey is unpleasant and drives relapse. If you use heavily, use strong extracts, mix substances, or have health conditions, a medically supported detox is safer.

mainEntity.name: Is kratom a good way to get off opioids?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is a risky substitution. People use kratom to ease off heroin or fentanyl but often end up dependent on kratom instead. Prescribed and monitored medications like buprenorphine-naloxone or methadone are safer and more effective.

mainEntity.name: What is the first step to getting help for kratom addiction?

acceptedAnswer.text: A simple, no-pressure conversation. An addiction assessment or a call to a confidential helpline helps you understand your options, then you can choose the level of care that fits, from a rapid access clinic to detox or a full treatment program.

blocks.text: Kratom is one of those substances that slips in through the side door. Nobody sets out to get hooked on a herbal powder they bought at a vape shop or ordered online. It starts as a way to take the edge off pain, to feel a little more energy, or to get through the day without opioids. Then one morning you skip a dose and your body lets you know, in no uncertain terms, that it now expects the drug.

blocks.text: If that sounds familiar, either for you or for someone you care about, you are not imagining it and you are not weak. Kratom acts on the same brain receptors as opioids like morphine and oxycodone, which means it can create real physical dependence and a withdrawal that feels a lot like the flu crossed with a panic attack. The encouraging part is that kratom dependence responds well to treatment, and Canadians have solid options for getting through it safely.

blocks.text: What is kratom?
blocks.html: What is kratom?

blocks.text: Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) is a tropical tree in the coffee family that grows across Southeast Asia, mainly Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Papua New Guinea. For generations, workers in those regions chewed the fresh leaves or brewed them into a tea to fight fatigue and ease aches. In North America it usually shows up as a dried green powder, packed into capsules, pressed into tablets, or sold as a concentrated extract.

blocks.text: Kratom leaves and powder contain mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, which act on the brain’s opioid receptors.
blocks.html: Kratom leaves and powder contain mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, which act on the brain’s opioid receptors.

blocks.text: The leaf contains dozens of active compounds, but two matter most. Mitragynine is the main one, and it makes up the bulk of the plant. The second, 7-hydroxymitragynine (often shortened to 7-OH), is present in tiny amounts naturally but is far more potent. Both bind to the body’s mu-opioid receptors, the same targets that prescription and street opioids hit. That is the whole story of why kratom can hook people the way it does.

blocks.text: Why people start using it
blocks.html: Why people start using it

blocks.text: Most people do not try kratom to get high. They reach for it because it promises to solve a problem. At low doses it acts more like a stimulant, giving a coffee-style lift and a mild sense of wellbeing. At higher doses the opioid effects take over, bringing pain relief, sedation, and calm.

blocks.text: Common reasons people give: managing chronic pain without a prescription, trying to self-treat anxiety or low mood, boosting energy and focus, and, very often, using kratom to blunt the withdrawal from stronger opioids. blocks.text: Is kratom legal in Canada?
blocks.html: Is kratom legal in Canada?

blocks.text: This is where things get confusing, because the answer is both yes and no. Kratom and its alkaloids are not scheduled under Canada’s Controlled Drugs and Substances Act. You will not be arrested for possessing it. But that does not make it an approved product.

blocks.text: Health Canada treats kratom as an unauthorized natural health product. It has not been approved for human consumption, so selling it as something to swallow, or advertising any health benefit, breaks the Food and Drugs Act and the Natural Health Products Regulations. That is why you see it sold as “incense,” “botanical specimen,” or “not for human consumption,” a wink-and-nod label that lets shops move the product while sidestepping the rules.

blocks.text: The 7-OH problem
blocks.html: The 7-OH problem

blocks.text: Regulators on both sides of the border have grown especially worried about 7-hydroxymitragynine. Because it is a much stronger opioid than plain leaf kratom, concentrated 7-OH products carry a higher risk of dependence and overdose. In July 2025, United States health agencies moved to classify synthetic 7-OH as a Schedule I controlled substance. Canada has not scheduled it as of 2026, but the direction of travel is clear, and these products are exactly the ones causing the most harm.

blocks.text: How kratom affects the brain and body
blocks.html: How kratom affects the brain and body

blocks.text: When mitragynine and 7-OH reach the brain, they latch onto mu-opioid receptors and nudge the reward and pain systems in an opioid-like direction. The body is remarkably good at adapting to this. After enough regular exposure it resets its own chemistry around the assumption that kratom will keep arriving. Natural endorphin production drops, receptors change, and the drug stops being a bonus and starts being a requirement just to feel normal.

blocks.text: This is tolerance and dependence, and it is a physical process, not a failure of character. Once it takes hold, stopping suddenly leaves the nervous system in a state of overdrive, which is what produces withdrawal. The same mechanism sits behind dependence on heroin, fentanyl, and prescription painkillers, which is why kratom withdrawal has such a familiar opioid shape.

blocks.text: Signs and symptoms of kratom addiction
blocks.html: Signs and symptoms of kratom addiction

blocks.text: Addiction, or opioid use disorder in clinical language, is more than just physical dependence. It is the loss of control, the continued use despite harm, and the way the substance starts crowding out everything else. With kratom, the signs often creep in slowly because the drug feels low-stakes and legal.

blocks.text: Kratom withdrawal: what to expect
blocks.html: Kratom withdrawal: what to expect

blocks.text: Because kratom works on opioid receptors, quitting after regular use sets off an opioid-type withdrawal. It is rarely life-threatening on its own, but it can be miserable, and the discomfort is the single biggest reason people give up and go back. Knowing what is coming, and having support lined up, changes the odds a lot.

blocks.html: Kratom withdrawal timeline

blocks.text: Everyone is a little different, but kratom withdrawal tends to follow a predictable arc. Symptoms usually begin within 12 to 24 hours of the last dose, peak somewhere around days two to four, and ease over the first week. Here is the general shape.

blocks.text: Post-acute withdrawal and why it matters
blocks.html: Post-acute withdrawal and why it matters

blocks.text: The physical worst is over in a week or so, but the brain takes longer to rebalance. Post-acute withdrawal syndrome, or PAWS, can bring stretches of low mood, patchy sleep, and cravings that arrive out of nowhere for weeks or even months. This is the phase where a lot of relapse happens, precisely because people assume they should feel fine by now and get blindsided when they do not. Ongoing counselling and support during this window is what protects the progress made in the first week. Understanding how detox fits into the larger recovery process helps set realistic expectations.

blocks.text: Health risks beyond dependence
blocks.html: Health risks beyond dependence

blocks.text: Kratom is often sold as a gentle, natural alternative, and that framing hides some real hazards. The United States Food and Drug Administration has warned for more than a decade that kratom is linked to liver damage, seizures, dependence, and, in some cases, death.

blocks.text: Liver, seizures, and overdose
blocks.html: Liver, seizures, and overdose

blocks.text: Case reports describe kratom-related liver injury, showing up as elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, and fatigue that resolves when the drug is stopped. Seizures have also been reported, more often at high doses or when kratom is mixed with other drugs. And because the alkaloids act on opioid receptors, very high doses, especially of potent 7-OH extracts, can slow breathing. Kratom poisonings reported to poison control centres have climbed sharply over the past decade as the products have grown stronger and more widespread.

blocks.text: The danger of mixing
blocks.html: The danger of mixing

blocks.text: Most serious kratom outcomes involve more than one substance. Combining it with alcohol, benzodiazepines, other opioids, or sedatives stacks up the effect on breathing and raises overdose risk. If kratom is being used alongside other drugs, that is all the more reason to detox with medical support rather than going it alone.

blocks.text: How kratom addiction is treated in Canada
blocks.html: How kratom addiction is treated in Canada

blocks.alt: Addiction counselor helping a client find kratom addiction treatment in Canada

blocks.text: Kratom dependence responds to the same proven treatments used for opioid use disorder across Canada.
blocks.html: Kratom dependence responds to the same proven treatments used for opioid use disorder across Canada.

blocks.text: Here is the reassuring part. Kratom dependence is treatable, and because it behaves like an opioid, it responds to the same well-established tools used for opioid use disorder. Treatment usually moves through a few stages, and the right mix depends on how severe the dependence is and what else is going on in a person’s life.

blocks.text: Step one: medically supervised detox
blocks.html: Step one: medically supervised detox

blocks.text: Detox is about getting through withdrawal safely and as comfortably as possible. In a medical detox setting, clinicians can ease symptoms with medication, keep you hydrated, monitor your heart rate and blood pressure, and step in if anything goes sideways. For anyone using heavily, using strong extracts, or mixing kratom with other substances, supervised detox in Canada is far safer and more bearable than quitting cold turkey at home. You can learn more about how a drug detox program is structured before you go in.

blocks.text: Step two: medication for cravings and withdrawal
blocks.html: Step two: medication for cravings and withdrawal

blocks.text: Opioid agonist therapy is the first-line treatment for opioid use disorder in Canada, and clinicians increasingly use it for significant kratom dependence too. Buprenorphine-naloxone, sold as Suboxone, is usually the preferred option because it settles cravings and withdrawal while carrying a lower overdose risk. It works on the very same receptors kratom targets, which is why it can smooth the transition off the drug so effectively. Methadone is another option for people with heavier opioid tolerance.

blocks.text: Step three: counselling and therapy
blocks.html: Step three: counselling and therapy

blocks.text: Medication handles the body. Therapy handles everything that drove the use in the first place. Cognitive behavioural therapy helps people spot the triggers and thought patterns that lead back to kratom, and build different responses. Because so many people start using kratom to self-treat pain, anxiety, or depression, addressing those underlying issues is central. When a mental health condition sits alongside the addiction, dual diagnosis treatment tackles both together rather than treating them as separate problems. Peer support, whether through a group program or a SMART Recovery meeting, gives people a place to stay honest and supported through the long tail of recovery.

blocks.text: Is kratom addictive?
blocks.html: Is kratom addictive?

blocks.text: Yes. Kratom’s main compounds act on opioid receptors, so regular use can lead to tolerance, physical dependence, and withdrawal. Heavier and longer use, especially of concentrated 7-OH extracts, raises the risk of a full opioid use disorder.

blocks.text: Is kratom legal in Canada?
blocks.html: Is kratom legal in Canada?

blocks.text: Kratom is not a controlled substance in Canada, so it is not illegal to possess. However, Health Canada has not authorized it for human consumption, so selling it as an ingestible product or making health claims about it is against the rules. The market is completely unregulated.

blocks.html: What is 7-hydroxymitragynine?

blocks.text: 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH, is a minor kratom alkaloid that is far more potent than the main compound, mitragynine. Concentrated 7-OH products are much stronger opioids and carry higher risks of dependence and overdose. Regulators have flagged them as a growing concern.

blocks.text: A note on sources and medical accuracy
blocks.html: A note on sources and medical accuracy

blocks.text: The information here draws on guidance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, published research on kratom pharmacology and withdrawal, and Canadian clinical practice for opioid use disorder, including opioid agonist therapy as described by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) and Health Canada’s work on the ongoing overdose crisis. Kratom research is still developing, and individual medical situations vary, so this article is educational and not a substitute for personal medical advice. If you are dependent on kratom or any opioid, please speak with a doctor or an addiction specialist before stopping, especially if you use other substances or have existing health conditions.
